sections.overview: The crescent betta is a small wild species native to parts of Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore and Sumatra. It belongs to the splendens group, close to B. splendens and B. mahachaiensis, and is a bubble-nesting fish rather than one of the mouthbrooding Bornean bettas.
sections.identification: It reaches about 6 cm standard length. The dark brown to black body, iridescent blue opercular scales and bright red crescent at the rear edge of the tail fin distinguish it from B. splendens; the latter commonly has different fin and body markings, especially in domestic forms.
sections.habitat: It inhabits shallow lowland wetlands, including stagnant pools, ditches, swamps and rice fields, in clear to brown fresh water. Its documented tolerance of modified habitats is broader than that of peat-swamp specialists such as B. brownorum.
sections.diet: It is a small carnivorous fish that takes aquatic insects and other tiny invertebrates. Its feeding ecology resembles that of other wild bettas, including B. splendens, even though the two species occupy different geographic and habitat settings.
sections.behavior: Males defend territories and can fight, although B. imbellis is generally less aggressive than selectively bred fighting strains of B. splendens. The name imbellis means unwarlike, but it does not mean the fish is invariably peaceful toward its own species.
sections.reproduction: The species builds a bubble nest. During spawning, eggs may sink briefly before being collected by one or both parents and placed in the foam nest, where the male guards them; this differs from the paternal mouthbrooding of B. channoides and B. edithae.
sections.ecology: Its broad distribution and ability to use ditches and rice fields help explain why its global risk is assessed differently from narrowly distributed peat-swamp relatives. Local wetland loss and pollution can still affect populations, so general resilience does not imply that every site is intact.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessment published in 2019 lists Betta imbellis as Least Concern. This is a global assessment and should not be read as a guarantee for every local population or wetland.
